title: Design a notification system
problem: Events must become pushes, texts and emails through providers you do not control, without duplicates, without ignoring a user's preferences, and without a marketing blast delaying a one-time password.
summary: A notification system is a durable queue first: events are deduplicated and filtered by preference, queued per channel and priority, sent by paced workers through provider adapters with retries and a dead-letter queue, and tracked through provider webhooks.
catTip: Treats arrive by post, text and pigeon. I sort urgent from junk before the couriers see them, never deliver the same treat twice, and if the pigeon service is down I keep the treat in the queue instead of losing it.

recall.q: A campaign makes 10k notifications a second arrive while the SMS provider accepts 500. What absorbs the difference, and how does an OTP avoid waiting behind the campaign?
recall.a: Durable queues absorb the spike, one per channel and priority, because neither Kafka nor SQS reorders by priority inside a queue. Workers drain the transactional lane first and the pacer reserves a slice of each provider's rate for it, so an OTP never waits for a marketing token.

guide.breaks: Calling providers synchronously from the API collapses at a 100× campaign spike, one shared queue puts one-time passwords behind coupons, and at-least-once redelivery sends the same text twice.
guide.tradeoffs: Everything after ingestion is asynchronous and eventually consistent, so the design carries three layers of idempotency, a pacer per provider, a reconciler that polls for stuck statuses, and queues that hold minutes of backlog by design.
guide.explainSimply: Think of a post office sorting floor: sacks of letters come in, get sorted into express and bulk bins for each destination, and leave on trucks that carry a fixed load an hour. Express always boards first, every letter is stamped so it cannot be sent twice, and undeliverable mail goes to a returns shelf instead of being thrown away.
guide.hint: Compare the arrival rate during a campaign with the rate each provider accepts, then ask what sits between them and how urgent work overtakes bulk.

meow: Urgent lane, bulk lane, one delivery per treat, and the pigeon gets a retry before I give up. Mew.

quiz.prompt: A marketing campaign of 2M pushes starts at 18:00 and OTP delivery latency rises from 2 s to 15 minutes. Which change fixes the cause?
options: Separate queues per channel and priority, with workers that drain the transactional lane first and a reserved slice of provider capacity
Switch the push queue from Kafka to SQS FIFO
quiz.explanation: The OTPs are waiting behind campaign messages in the same queue, so only a separate lane with priority drains them first. More workers is the strongest distractor: it helps only until the provider's accepted rate, and the OTPs still queue behind the campaign; FIFO makes ordering stricter, not smarter.

quiz.prompt: A worker crashes after APNs accepted a push but before it recorded the status, and the queue redelivers the message. What keeps the user from receiving two pushes?
options: Kafka exactly-once transactions on the push topic
A claim-before-send update on the delivery row (a lease) plus the provider's collapse id, accepting that a crash in the narrow window may still resend
Deleting the queue message before calling the provider
quiz.explanation: Only a row-level claim stops a second worker from sending, and a collapse id makes a rare resend harmless on the device. Kafka transactions are the strongest distractor, but they cover Kafka-to-Kafka work, not an HTTP call to a provider; deleting before sending turns a crash into a lost notification.

cards.q: Problem: queues are at-least-once and a provider call cannot be undone. Decision?
cards.a: Layer idempotency: a unique idempotency key at the API, Redis SET NX with a TTL at ingestion, a claim-before-send update with a lease on the delivery row, and provider collapse ids (APNs apns-collapse-id, FCM collapse key) where they exist. Decide per priority what a crash in the remaining window does: resend an OTP, drop a marketing message.

cards.q: Problem: a campaign sends 100× the normal rate while OTPs must still arrive in seconds. Decision?
cards.a: Queues per channel and priority (sms-high, sms-bulk) because neither Kafka nor SQS has per-message priority; workers drain high first with weighted polling as a starvation guard; the per-provider pacer reserves a slice of the accepted rate for the high lane; campaign fan-out is paced at the provider's rate so backlog stays bounded; preferences are re-checked at send time.

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation, "Sending notification requests to APNs"
sources.supports: HTTP/2 with long-lived reusable connections and advice to spread pushes across connections; apns-expiration (0 means a single attempt, no storage; stored up to 30 days otherwise); apns-priority 10, 5 and 1; apns-collapse-id up to 64 bytes merges notifications; APNs stores only one notification per bundle id per device, usually the latest; payload limit of 4 KB

sources.title: Apple Developer Documentation, "Handling notification responses from APNs"
sources.supports: status 410 Unregistered with a timestamp when a token is no longer active; 429 TooManyRequests for the same device token; TooManyProviderTokenUpdates (update the token no more than once every 20 minutes); retry 5xx responses after a wait with back-off; do not retry BadDeviceToken, Unregistered, ExpiredToken or PayloadTooLarge

sources.title: Firebase documentation, "FCM HTTP v1 API: ErrorCode"
sources.supports: UNREGISTERED (404): remove the token; QUOTA_EXCEEDED (429): exponential backoff with a minimum initial delay of one minute; UNAVAILABLE (503): honour Retry-After, otherwise exponential backoff with jitter; INTERNAL (500): retry; TTL range 0 to 2,419,200 seconds

sources.title: Firebase documentation, "Set the lifespan of a message"
sources.supports: messages without a ttl last up to four weeks by default; ttl of 0 discards messages that cannot be delivered immediately; maximum 2,419,200 seconds (28 days)

sources.title: Firebase documentation, "Non-collapsible and collapsible messages"
sources.supports: a collapsible message may be replaced by a newer one with the same collapse key before delivery; at most four collapse keys per registration token at a time

sources.title: AWS, "Amazon SQS visibility timeout" (Developer Guide)
sources.supports: default visibility timeout of 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours; a message not deleted before the timeout becomes visible again; at-least-once delivery means a message may still be delivered more than once

sources.title: AWS, "Amazon SQS queue types" (Developer Guide)
sources.supports: standard queues: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering; FIFO queues: exactly-once processing with MessageDeduplicationId, 300 API calls per second per action, 3,000 messages per second with batching, 30,000 TPS in high-throughput mode

sources.title: AWS, "Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS" (Developer Guide)
sources.supports: redrive policy with maxReceiveCount; for standard queues the original enqueue timestamp is kept when a message moves to the DLQ, so the DLQ's retention should be longer than the source queue's

sources.title: AWS, "Amazon SQS features"
sources.supports: "Priority: Use separate queues to provide prioritization of work"

sources.title: Ricardo Ferreira, "Implementing Message Prioritization in Apache Kafka" (Confluent blog, 10 September 2020)
sources.supports: Kafka has no native message prioritisation because records in the commit log are immutable and the broker never reorders them; the bucket-priority pattern as a workaround

sources.title: Twilio documentation, "Track the message status of outbound messages"
sources.supports: status callbacks are POST requests to a StatusCallback URL on each status change (queued, sent, delivered, undelivered, failed) with MessageSid, MessageStatus and ErrorCode; callbacks are not guaranteed to arrive in order; signature validation recommended

sources.title: Twilio documentation, "Best practices for outbound message delivery status logging"
sources.supports: poll the API if a message has not reached delivered or undelivered within 12 hours; reconcile statuses at least daily

sources.title: Twilio documentation, "Error 30001: Queue overflow"
sources.supports: messages sent faster than a sender's throughput are queued; messages can only be queued for 10 hours before they automatically fail; default validity period of 36,000 seconds

sources.title: Twilio SendGrid documentation, "Event Webhook reference"
sources.supports: delivery events processed, dropped, delivered, deferred and bounce; engagement events open, click, spam report, unsubscribe; sg_event_id for deduplication; the signed event webhook and OAuth 2.0 for securing it

sources.title: AWS, "Managing your Amazon SES sending limits" (Developer Guide)
sources.supports: sending quota per 24 hours and maximum send rate per second; sandbox accounts limited to 200 messages per 24 hours and one message per second; quotas raised on request

sources.title: Redis documentation, "SET" command
sources.supports: SET with NX sets the key only if it does not exist and returns a null reply otherwise; EX sets the expiry in seconds

sources.title: Paul Tarjan, "Scaling your API with rate limiters" (Stripe Engineering, 30 March 2017)
sources.supports: the fleet usage load shedder reserves a share of capacity for critical traffic, with 20% given as an example
